summary: Defines a YANG data model for managing radio link interfaces in a microwave or millimeter wave node, and for their connection to packet (typically Ethernet) interfaces. Interface protection is split into a separate generic model so it can be reused for other interface types. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: The settings sheet for a radio dish that sends data through the air from tower to tower, written in a form software can read and change.

subtitle: A YANG model for configuring and monitoring microwave radio links, plus a reusable interface protection model.

tldr.problem: Microwave and millimeter wave radio equipment from different vendors needs a common, machine-readable way to be configured and monitored.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8561 defines three YANG modules. They extend the standard interfaces model with a Radio Link Terminal and Carrier Terminations, add a generic interface protection module, and define the coding and modulation types.
tldr.outcome: Operators can manage frequencies, power, modulation, protection, XPIC and MIMO through NETCONF or RESTCONF using one model. The protection module can be reused for other interface types.

today: RFC 8561 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this RFC.

sections.title: What the Model Covers
sections.content:
RFC 8561 defines a YANG data model for management and control of radio link interfaces, and their relationship to packet (typically Ethernet) and Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) interfaces, in a microwave or millimeter wave node. It builds on the ETSI EN 302217 series, in particular part 2, which covers systems from 1.4 GHz to 86 GHz.

The model has configuration and state data under the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342). Its design follows the framework in RFC 8432, which includes a gap analysis of existing models. The structure is based on the IETF Radio Link Model and augments the interface model of RFC 8343 so that radio links are managed like other interfaces.

The interface protection data nodes are split out into a separate, generic module so that other interface types can use them too.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every radio maker inventing its own settings screen, they all agree on one list of settings that software can read and change.

sections.title: Radio Link Terminals and Carrier Terminations
sections.content:
Two terms carry the design. A Carrier Termination (CT) is an interface for the capacity provided over the air by a single carrier. It is typically defined by its transmitting and receiving frequencies. A Radio Link Terminal (RLT) is an interface that provides packet and/or TDM capacity to the associated Ethernet and/or TDM interfaces in a node, and is used to set up a transport service over a microwave link.

The model uses interface layering from RFC 8343. An RLT interface (type microwaveRadioLinkTerminal) lists the CT interfaces (type microwaveCarrierTermination) it contains. The RLT mode is written as X plus Y, where X is the number of bonded carrier terminations and Y is the number of protecting ones. The module defines one-plus-zero, one-plus-one and two-plus-zero.

Some generic interface leafs do not apply. The enabled leaf is not applicable to an RLT, since enabling and disabling is done in the constituent CTs. Packet counters such as in-octets and out-errors are outside the scope of the radio link domain and do not apply to RLT and CT.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of one big road made of several lanes. Each lane is a radio channel, and the road as a whole is what the network sees. You switch lanes on and off individually, not the whole road.

sections.title: Carrier Parameters and Status
sections.content:
Each carrier termination has the settings an engineer would expect. tx-frequency and channel-separation are mandatory and given in kHz. The receive side is set either directly with rx-frequency or by a duplex-distance subtracted from the transmit frequency. A polarization can be horizontal, vertical or not specified. The transmitter is switched with tx-enabled, which defaults to false, and tx-oper-status reports off, on or standby.

Power control is a choice between fixed RTPC (remote transmit power control) with a maximum nominal power, and ATPC (automatic transmitter power control) with a maximum plus lower and upper thresholds. Coding and modulation is either a single selected scheme or an adaptive range with a minimum and maximum (selected-min-acm and selected-max-acm). Power values use a one-decimal-place decimal type.

Read-only data reports the actual transmitted and received levels, actual modulation, signal-to-noise-plus-interference, device capabilities, and error statistics (BBE, ES, SES and UAS counters). It also reports radio performance statistics such as minimum and maximum received and transmitted level. Alarm thresholds, IF loops and RF loops can be configured.
sections.plainLanguage: For each radio channel you pick the tune it plays, how loud it is, and how fancy its code is. The radio also reports back how loud it hears the other side and how many mistakes it made.

sections.title: Protection, XPIC and MIMO
sections.content:
Protection is defined in a separate module, ietf-interface-protection, which references ITU-T G.808.1. A protection group has a name, a protection architecture type, and at least two member interfaces. The architecture is either one-plus-one-type (one interface protects another) or one-to-n-type (one interface protects n others), with 1+1 as the default. The group also has a revertive wait-to-restore time, a hold-off timer, and a status of unprotected, protected or unable-to-protect.

The protection group exposes actions an operator can invoke: manual-switch-working, manual-switch-protection, forced-switch, lockout-of-protection, freeze, exercise and clear.

The radio link module also defines optional features. xpic (Cross Polarization Interference Cancellation) groups carriers in pairs, mimo (Multiple Input Multiple Output) groups carriers in MIMO groups, and tdm enables TDM connections on the RLT. A third module, ietf-microwave-types, defines the identities for RLT modes and for coding and modulation, from BPSK and QPSK through QAM up to 4096 states, with strong and light variants.
sections.plainLanguage: If one radio breaks, a spare takes over, like a spare tire. The model also lets you pair up radios that talk on different polarizations so they do not disturb each other.

sections.title: Worked Configuration Examples
sections.content:
Appendix A shows three illustrative instances: 1+0, 2+0 and 2+0 with XPIC. They are examples, not complete configurations.

In the 1+0 example, the near-end node has one RLT in mode one-plus-zero containing one carrier termination. That CT has a tx-frequency of 10728000, a duplex-distance of 644000, a channel-separation of 28000, a maximum nominal RTPC power of 20 and a single coding and modulation scheme of qam-512. The RLT also carries 4 E1 TDM connections.

In the 2+0 XPIC example, the RLT is in mode two-plus-zero with two carrier terminations that are also listed as an XPIC pair.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are filled-in forms. They show what the settings for one radio, or two radios working as a team, would look like.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are meant to be accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). Their mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH (RFC 6242) and TLS (RFC 8446). The NETCONF Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

Writable data nodes can be sensitive. The RLT mode, its carrier terminations, protection groups, XPIC pairs, MIMO groups and TDM connections must match the configuration of the far end. Carrier settings such as frequencies, channel separation, power thresholds, modulation, and IF and RF loops must match too. In each case the RFC warns that unauthorized access could interrupt the ability to forward traffic.

The protection actions are also sensitive, since unauthorized use could interrupt forwarding or remove the ability to perform a necessary protection switch. The security considerations of RFC 8343 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing a radio's settings by mistake or on purpose can cut the link. So only the right people should be allowed to touch them, over a locked connection.
